source_read: PMC HTML, PMC6055296 (Public Health Rep 2018;133(4):423–431), read in full in the reader's own browser tab (title confirmed): abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 1–2, discussion including Strengths and Weaknesses, conclusions, references. Figures 1–3 not viewed (no claim value is printed only in a figure). Table 2 columns summed and Table 1 rows recomputed by the reader.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source. The reallocated deaths are potential opioid-related deaths under an untested equal-proportion assumption, and the claim says so; the authors' own conclusion (official figures may substantially understate the problem) is stronger than the claim. The editors' 45% understates rather than overstates multi-drug coding.
claims.note: Every Buchanich number in the statement and magnitude checks: 97,159 of 438,607 (22.2%); District of Columbia 0% and Pennsylvania 50.8% in 2015; over 70,000 reallocated in 1999–2015; 5,662 in 2015 is the reader's sum of Table 2's reallocated column (the text says only over 5,600; the reported column sums to 29,383, the national 2015 count); Pennsylvania 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (+103%, about double). Editors' 45% recomputes as 115,192 of 255,527 = 45.1% if 'another drug's code' means a specific non-opioid code; counting T50.9 co-codes gives 62.6%, and the opioid-type shares sum to 115.8%, so more deaths carried a second opioid code: 45% is a lower bound and 'a non-opioid drug's code' would be exact. Points for the editor: (1) 'named none' here means T50.9 was the only drug code; T50.9 is also used for drugs without a code of their own (e.g. bath salts), which the authors judge a very small share, and 313 further deaths had no T code at all. (2) For this correction 'similar deaths' means only the same state and year. (3) The paper describes its denominator inconsistently (Methods 4th paragraph: deaths with a specified drug; the same paragraph's restatement, the Table 2 footnote and the Figure 3 caption: all overdose deaths); Table 2 arithmetic shows the specified-drug denominator was used, which is what the claim says. (4) Discussion 1st paragraph gives the five largest states' share as 15,247 of 32,860 reallocated deaths, which contradicts both the 70,000 total and Pennsylvania's own 11,152; a rough national check (97,159 × 255,527/341,135 ≈ 72,800) supports the 70,000. (5) Abstract typo: unspecified deaths rose to 7,227, not 29,383. Outside this task file: Discussion 3rd paragraph reports that in 2015 states with a central medical examiner had lower unspecified shares than other systems, but not significantly (relevant to cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates).

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Total column and footnote f)
anchors.extracted: US unintentional drug overdose deaths (underlying cause X40–X44, NVSS multiple-cause files), 1999–2015: 438,607. By contributory T codes: opioid-related 255,527 (58%), non-opioid only 85,608 (20%), unspecified (T50.9 the only drug code) 97,159 (22%); 313 with no T code. Unspecified deaths 2,255 in 1999, 7,227 in 2015, peak 8,145 in 2011. Reader's check: 97,159/438,607 = 22.2%.

T50.9 used alone indicates that no drug was reported on the certificate, but the code is also used for drugs with no specific code (e.g. bath salts); the authors judge this a very small share. Only unintentional deaths analysed: suicide, homicide and undetermined-intent drug deaths excluded.

2015: more than 35% of unintentional overdose deaths unspecified in Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Alabama, Indiana and Mississippi; 17 states under 5%; District of Columbia no unspecified deaths; Pennsylvania highest at 50.8%.
Between 1999 and 2015 the unspecified share fell in 35 states (decreases of 0.2% in Louisiana to 42.2% in North Dakota) and rose in 16 (0.2% in New Mexico to 12.8% in New Jersey).

Correction: for each state and year, opioid-related unintentional deaths as a proportion of deaths with a specified drug, multiplied by that state-year's unspecified deaths, added to reported opioid deaths as potential opioid-related deaths. The restatement in the same paragraph, the Table 2 footnote and the Figure 3 caption give the denominator as all overdose deaths, but Table 2 matches the specified-drug denominator: Pennsylvania 1,307/(1,268 + 1,307) = 50.8%, its printed unspecified share (an all-deaths denominator would give about 644 reallocated, not 1,307).

Reallocation moved more than 70,000 unspecified deaths (1999–2015) to opioid-related, from 9 in Vermont to 11,152 in Pennsylvania; opioid-related counts more than doubled in Alabama, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Pennsylvania; California, Florida and Pennsylvania each gained more than 5,000 (totals 30,813, 25,144 and 20,521).

anchors.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2 (Pennsylvania row; reallocated-deaths column)
anchors.extracted: 2015: Pennsylvania 1,268 reported opioid-related unintentional deaths plus 1,307 reallocated; rate 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (+103%; text 9.9 to 20.1); rates rose more than 50% in Alabama, Indiana, Mississippi, Louisiana and Pennsylvania and less than 1% in five jurisdictions. Reader's sum of the 51 reallocated values = 5,662; reported values sum to 29,383.

Authors: potentially more than 70,000 unspecified unintentional deaths over 17 years, over 5,600 of them in 2015, could be opioid-related. The same paragraph says the five states with most reallocated deaths held 46.4% (15,247 of 32,860) of them, a total that conflicts with the 70,000 and with Pennsylvania's 11,152 plus over 5,000 each in California and Florida; reader's rough national check 97,159 × 255,527/341,135 ≈ 72,800 agrees with the 70,000.

The equal-proportion assumption is called 'rather strong' and was not tested (authors suggest comparing age, race, sex and geography of deaths with and without a named drug); no difference in reporting between certifiers assumed; drug reporting may depend on how much toxicology testing was done, postmortem redistribution, certifier experience and jurisdiction size, none of which the data show.

Opioid-related deaths 255,527: opioid code only 95,467; plus a non-opioid code 59,410; plus T50.9 44,868; plus both 55,782. Reader's calculation: with a specific non-opioid drug code 115,192 = 45.1%; with a non-opioid code or T50.9 160,060 = 62.6%. Opioid-type shares (pain relievers 41.5%, heroin 25.4%, methadone 20.3%, other/unspecified narcotics 14.4%, synthetics 14.2%, opium 0.01%) sum to 115.8%, so at least 15.8% carried two or more opioid codes.

ICD-10 drug-class codes lose specificity even with complete certificates (fentanyl analogues all coded T40.4); new synthetic drugs may not be detected by toxicology and are then not written on the certificate.
Only unintentional deaths analysed; the undetermined share varies by state, so states with many undetermined deaths were less affected by the reallocation.
